claim: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) affects approximately 1% of women under forty years of age.
source: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) affects ~1% of women under forty.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction without specific experimental data from this study, but is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Exome sequencing of two Finnish sisters with non-syndromic POI revealed a homozygous mutation in FANCM leading to p.Gln1701* truncation.
source: Exome sequencing of two Finnish sisters with non-syndromic POI revealed a homozygous mutation in FANCM, leading to a truncated protein (p.Gln1701*).
evidence: The manuscript presents whole-exome sequencing data showing the mutation in both sisters, confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

claim: The patients' lymphocytes displayed higher levels of basal and mitomycin C (MMC)-induced chromosomal abnormalities compared to the mother's cells.
source: Compared to the mother's cells, the patients' lymphocytes displayed higher levels of basal and mitomycin C (MMC)-induced chromosomal abnormalities.
evidence: Figure 3A and B show chromosome breakage analysis data comparing patients and mother.

claim: The patients' lymphoblasts were hypersensitive to MMC.
source: Their lymphoblasts were hypersensitive to MMC
evidence: Figure 3D shows growth inhibition data demonstrating MMC hypersensitivity.

claim: MMC-induced monoubiquitination of FANCD2 was impaired in the patients' cells.
source: MMC-induced monoubiquitination of FANCD2 was impaired.
evidence: Western blot data in Figures 3C and 4A demonstrate impaired FANCD2 monoubiquitination in response to MMC.

claim: Genetic complementation of patient's cells with wild-type FANCM improved their resistance to MMC.
source: Genetic complementation of patient's cells with wild-type FANCM improved their resistance to MMC re-establishing FANCD2 monoubiquitination.
evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that transduction with wild-type FANCM cDNA restored MMC resistance and FANCD2 monoubiquitination.

claim: FANCM was more strongly expressed in human fetal germ cells than in somatic cells.
source: FANCM was more strongly expressed in human fetal germ cells than in somatic cells.
evidence: Figure 2B shows qRT-PCR data from sorted germ cells (D2-40+) versus somatic cells (D2-40-) demonstrating higher FANCM expression in germ cells.

claim: FANCM protein was preferentially expressed along the chromosomes in pachytene cells, which undergo meiotic recombination.
source: FANCM protein was preferentially expressed along the chromosomes in pachytene cells, which undergo meiotic recombination.
evidence: Figure 2C and 2D show immunohistochemistry data demonstrating FANCM localization along chromosomes in pachytene stage oocytes.

claim: This is the first documented Mendelian phenotype due to a biallelic FANCM mutation.
source: Our findings document the first Mendelian phenotype due to a biallelic FANCM mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and comparison with existing literature.

claim: Resumption of ovarian function occurs in approximately 24% of POI cases.
source: Infertility is usually definitive but resumption of ovarian function occurs in ~24% of cases (Tucker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Tucker et al., 2016.

claim: POI remains idiopathic in approximately 70% of cases.
source: POI is etiologically heterogeneous (OMIM: ODG1 # 233300. ODG2 # 300510 ODG3 # 614324, ODG4 # 616185) and remains idiopathic in ~70% of the cases
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: FANCM is a DNA-damage response gene whose heterozygous mutations predispose to breast cancer.
source: FANCM is a DNA-damage response gene whose heterozygous mutations predispose to breast cancer.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The products of 21 genes (FANCA to FANCV) whose loss-of-function has been associated with FA are subdivided into three functional groups.
source: The products of the 21 genes (FANCA to FANCV) whose loss-of-function has been associated to FA are subdivided into three functional groups (Bogliolo and Surrallés, 2015; Ceccaldi et al., 2016; Wang, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: FANCM has been excluded from the group of FA genes based on recent analysis.
source: However, a more recent analysis reconsidered the role of some FA-associated genes in the establishment of bona fide FA clinical and cellular phenotypes and excluded FANCM from the group of FA genes (Bogliolo and Surrallés, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Bogliolo and Surrallés, 2015.

claim: The phenotypes associated with FANCM biallelic mutations thus far are cancer predisposition, particularly early-onset breast cancer in females, and chemosensitivity.
source: The phenotypes associated to FANCM biallelic mutations thus far are cancer predisposition, in particular early-onset breast cancer in females, and chemosensitivity. (Michl et al., 2016; Bogliolo et al., 2017; Catucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: The FANCM mutation identified is c.5101C>T, resulting in p.Gln1701* truncation.
source: Here, we have performed a whole-exome sequencing in a Finnish family with two patients presenting with non-syndromic POI and identified a homozygous truncating mutation (c.5101C>T; p.Gln1701*) in FANCM
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by sequencing data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The two POI patients belong to a consanguineous family without history of cancer.
source: The two POI patients belong to a consanguineous family (Figure 1A) without history of cancer.

claim: Both patients had normal pilosity, breast and external genitalia, normal blood counts and liver balance, and had normal high-resolution karyotype and FMR1 gene.
source: Both patients had normal pilosity, breast and external genitalia, normal blood counts and liver balance, and had normal high-resolution karyotype and FMR1 gene.

source: Proband had menarche at 12 years of age, with irregular cycles (20–60 days).

claim: Patient 2 had menarche at 12 years of age with regular menses (23 days).

claim: Patient 2 became spontaneously pregnant and gave birth to a healthy child.
source: However, about 6 months later, she became spontaneously pregnant and gave birth to a healthy child.

claim: The FANCM variant chr14:45658326 C/T (rs147021911) was the only variant fulfilling the filtering criteria in the exome sequencing analysis.
source: The only variant fulfilling these criteria was the non-sense mutation chr14:45658326 C/T (rs147021911) in exon 20 of FANCM (Figure 1B, Tables 2–3).
evidence: This is stated based on the exome sequencing data analysis shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The FANCM variant has a minor allele frequency (MAF) of 0.0013 in the general population and 0.0089 in the Finnish population according to the ExAC database.
source: According to the ExAC database, its MAF is 0.0013, slightly higher in the Finnish population (0.0089)
evidence: This is cited from the ExAC database.

claim: Only one homozygous individual for the FANCM variant is described in the ExAC database.
source: with only one homozygous individual described in the ExAC database.
evidence: This is cited from the ExAC database.

claim: The p.Gln1701* truncation removes the C-terminal endonuclease and the FAAP24-interaction domain from FANCM protein.
source: This variant leads to the p.Gln1701* truncation at the protein level, which removes the C-terminal endonuclease and the FA associated protein 24 (FAAP24)-interaction domain (Figure 1D).

claim: FAAP24 mediates chromatin association of FANCM.
source: FAAP24 mediates chromatin association of FANCM.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge.

claim: Immunoblot confirmed the expression of a truncated FANCM protein of approximately 195 kDa in the cell line derived from patient 2.
source: Immunoblot with an anti-FANCM antibody confirmed the expression of a truncated FANCM protein of ~195 kDa in the cell line derived from the patient

source: whereas both the wild-type/WT (MW ~235 kDa) and the truncated proteins were present in the heterozygous mother (Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1E shows Western blot data demonstrating both protein forms in the mother.

claim: The expression level of the truncated FANCM protein was significantly reduced compared to the wild-type.
source: The expression level of the truncated protein was significantly reduced compared to the WT

source: suggesting that the mutation destabilizes either the protein or the corresponding mRNA (i.e., non-sense mediated decay).

claim: No variants were observed in other FANC genes in the exome sequencing analysis.
source: No variants were observed in other FANC genes.
evidence: Table 4 shows comprehensive analysis of all FANC pathway genes with no causative variants found.

source: qRT-PCR in human fetal ovaries demonstrated that FANCM mRNAs were expressed throughout ovarian development (5–32 weeks post-fertilization, wpf) (Figure 2A).

claim: FANCM protein was present in the nuclei of oogonia with stronger staining in pachytene stage oocytes.

claim: FANCM staining localized along the chromosomes in pachytene cells that undergo meiotic recombination.
source: Of note, staining localized along the chromosomes in pachytene cells that undergo meiotic recombination.

claim: FANCM was observed in oocytes arrested at the diplotene stage of prophase I during the last trimester of pregnancy and in adults.
source: FANCM was also observed in oocytes arrested at the diplotene stage of prophase I during the last trimester of pregnancy and in adults (Figure 2C).

evidence: Figure 2D shows co-staining immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Baseline chromosome breakage and rearrangement occurrence was higher in both POI patients than in their mother.

source: The reduced level of FANCD2 in lymphocytes from POI patients is likely due to a reduced proliferation of their cells in culture conditions.
